summary: Trientine hydrochloride is an oral copper-chelating agent indicated for Wilson's disease in patients who are intolerant of penicillamine. It is not interchangeable with penicillamine and, lacking a sulfhydryl group, is ineffective in cystinuria or rheumatoid arthritis. It binds excess copper and increases its urinary excretion. Trientine must be taken on an empty stomach, away from food, milk, and other medicines, because it chelates metals such as iron. Iron deficiency is the most notable adverse effect; treatment response is followed by free serum copper and 24-hour urinary copper.
indications: Treatment of Wilson's disease in patients who are intolerant of penicillamine

moa: Trientine (triethylenetetramine) is a polyamine chelating agent that contains amine groups capable of forming a stable complex with cupric (copper) ions. By chelating the excess copper that accumulates in Wilson's disease, it promotes the elimination of copper through urinary excretion, lowering the body's copper burden. Unlike penicillamine it lacks a sulfhydryl moiety, so it cannot bind cystine and is therefore ineffective in cystinuria. Its chelating action is not specific to copper and it may also bind other metals such as iron, which underlies the need to avoid concurrent iron and to dose on an empty stomach.

absolute: Rheumatoid arthritis (not indicated; not a substitute for penicillamine)
relative: Concurrent oral iron therapy (chelation reduces both)
monitor: Free serum copper and 24-hour urinary copper

preg: There are limited data; trientine may cause fetal harm and copper is essential for normal development, so over-chelation could be harmful. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed, with careful monitoring of maternal copper status to maintain it within the desired range.
lact: It is not known whether trientine hydrochloride is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a nursing infant, use caution and weigh the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Pharmacokinetic data on trientine are not available and no specific renal dose adjustment is defined; dosing is guided by clinical response and copper indices rather than renal function.
hepatic: Trientine is used specifically to manage the copper overload of Wilson's disease, which involves the liver; it is not indicated for primary biliary cirrhosis. Monitor hepatic status and copper indices and adjust dose to clinical response.

major: Oral iron salts - trientine chelates iron and both drugs' absorption is reduced; if iron is needed, give it at a different time and only for short periods
moderate: Mineral supplements (zinc, calcium, magnesium) and antacids - reduced trientine absorption; separate dosing
Other oral medications - general reduction in absorption when taken together; separate by at least 1 hour
minor: Foods rich in copper (liver, shellfish, chocolate, nuts) - may counteract copper depletion goals
interactions.food: Must be taken on an empty stomach away from food and milk, which markedly reduce absorption.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction reported; limit alcohol in hepatic disease.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor free serum copper and 24-hour urinary copper to assess adequacy of chelation.

serious: Worsening neurological symptoms (dystonia, muscular spasm) during initiation
rare: Heartburn, gastritis, melena (reported in non-Wilson use)

monitoring: Complete blood count and iron status for iron deficiency
Neurologic and hepatic clinical status, reviewed every 6-12 months
counsel: Take this medicine on an empty stomach, at least one hour before or two hours after meals
Do not take it with milk, antacids, iron or mineral supplements, or other medicines - separate them by at least an hour
Swallow capsules whole; if contents touch your skin, wash the area with water
Report worsening tremor, stiffness, fatigue, or signs of anemia
Keep all appointments for blood and urine copper tests - your dose is adjusted from them
pk: Reduction of copper burden develops over weeks of therapy
Quantitative pharmacokinetic data are not available
Dosed two to four times daily for ongoing copper control
Store refrigerated at 2-8 C; keep tightly closed and protect from light
pearls: Reserved for Wilson's disease patients intolerant of penicillamine; the two are NOT interchangeable
Lacks a sulfhydryl group, so it is useless in cystinuria (unlike penicillamine)
Must be given on an empty stomach, away from food, milk, iron, and other drugs
Iron deficiency is the characteristic adverse effect; give iron only briefly and at a separate time
Adjust the dose using free serum copper (~10-25 mcg/dL) and 24-hour urinary copper, not symptoms alone
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on an empty stomach. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed one and continue your usual schedule. Do not take two doses together.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Acute overdose may cause gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting); excessive long-term chelation can lead to copper deficiency with anemia and neutropenia. There is no specific antidote; manage with supportive care, monitor copper status, and consider copper supplementation if over-depletion is documented.
